alternatives: Lorazepam (or oxazepam by nasogastric tube) in place of chlordiazepoxide or diazepam for withdrawal.
contraindications: Chlordiazepoxide and diazepam: long-acting, with active metabolites that accumulate in severe liver disease; avoid.
interactions: Lactulose, rifaximin and thiamine: no clinically relevant interaction with the current medicines.
Sertraline in severe hepatic impairment (Child-Pugh C): exposure is increased; the product label does not recommend use in moderate or severe hepatic impairment.
Sertraline: can cause hyponatremia (SIADH) and impairs platelet aggregation; relevant with sodium 128 mEq/L, platelets 48 x10^9/L and grade II varices.
Furosemide and spironolactone: with potassium 2.8 mEq/L, sodium 128 mEq/L and creatinine 1.4 mg/dL, diuretics worsen the electrolyte and renal disorders that precipitate hepatic encephalopathy.
Propranolol: blunts the heart-rate response to withdrawal, bleeding and infection; reduce or hold if systolic BP falls below 90 mmHg or kidney injury progresses.
Any benzodiazepine with hepatic encephalopathy: additive central nervous system depression; can deepen encephalopathy.

action_criteria.label: Core laboratory work-up: blood count, electrolytes, renal and liver function, glucose, INR, ammonia and CRP, with toxicology where alcohol or drugs are in question
action_criteria.rationale: Confirms liver dysfunction and identifies metabolic, nutritional and toxic precipitants after an alcohol binge [ACG_HE_2026]

action_criteria.rationale: Infection is the commonest precipitant of overt HE and can be occult in cirrhosis; this patient is afebrile with a normal white cell count and no focal source, so the screen is recommended rather than required (EASL 2022).

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Sertraline is unsuitable in Child-Pugh C and worsens the low sodium and the bleeding risk; spironolactone and furosemide are stopped; short-acting lorazepam or oxazepam replaces long-acting agents for withdrawal.
action_criteria.label: Medication review of sertraline, diuretics and propranolol, and choice of benzodiazepine for alcohol withdrawal in Child-Pugh C cirrhosis
action_criteria.rationale: Hepatic dosing of sertraline, the diuretics in hypokalemia and hyponatremia, and the benzodiazepine for the withdrawal that will follow the binge all change management [EASL_ALD_2018]

prohibited_recommendations: Do not give scheduled or long-acting benzodiazepines; treat alcohol withdrawal symptom-triggered with the lowest effective dose of lorazepam or oxazepam and close monitoring of consciousness (EASL ALD 2018).
Do not prescribe opioids or other sedating drugs: they precipitate and prolong HE; for pain use acetaminophen up to 2 g per day.
Do not attribute the coma to alcohol intoxication alone and wait for the ethanol to clear: start HE treatment, airway protection and the precipitant work-up now.
Do not restrict dietary protein: malnutrition worsens HE and outcome (EASL 2022).
required_recommendations: Protect the airway: GCS 8 with a reduced gag reflex and tense ascites; admit to the ICU and intubate for airway protection before nasogastric treatment.

Identify and treat the precipitant: the alcohol binge with lactulose and rifaximin non-adherence, with hypokalemia and hypoglycemia as co-precipitants; screen for infection (paracentesis, blood and urine cultures, chest radiograph for aspiration after being found down) and treat any infection found; repeat the chest radiograph if fever or hypoxaemia develops after intubation.

Give thiamine 200 mg IV three times daily (EFNS 2010) immediately, before or with the dextrose that corrects the hypoglycemia (glucose 58 mg/dL); do not delay the glucose, and monitor capillary glucose.

Lactulose 25 mL every 1-2 hours until at least two soft bowel movements, then titrated to 2-3 soft bowel movements per day (ACG 2026 recommendation 10; EASL 2022), by nasogastric tube once the airway is secured or as a retention enema (300 mL lactulose in 700 mL water) until then; avoid over-titration, which causes dehydration, hypokalemia and kidney injury.
Restart rifaximin 550 mg twice daily with lactulose for this recurrent overt episode (ACG 2026; EASL 2022).

Replace potassium to 4.0 mEq/L or more, because hypokalemia increases renal ammoniagenesis, and replace magnesium (1.1 mg/dL) intravenously, with ECG monitoring; hold furosemide and spironolactone while overt HE, hypokalemia and hyponatremia persist (EASL 2018).

Monitor for alcohol withdrawal as the ethanol clears: CIWA-Ar cannot be scored while he is comatose or intubated, so use ICU sedation and autonomic monitoring, and treat withdrawal symptom-triggered with the lowest effective dose of lorazepam (EASL ALD 2018).

Hold sertraline (not recommended in severe hepatic impairment; adds to hyponatremia and bleeding risk with platelets 48) and review propranolol, reducing or holding it if systolic BP falls below 90 mmHg or kidney injury progresses (Baveno VII).
Tense ascites: large-volume paracentesis with albumin 8 g per litre removed (EASL 2018).
Once the acute episode is controlled, start primary SBP prophylaxis (norfloxacin 400 mg daily or ciprofloxacin): ascitic protein 0.8 g/dL with Child-Pugh C and bilirubin above 3 mg/dL (EASL 2018).

Assess with hepatology for superimposed severe alcohol-related hepatitis (recent heavy drinking, bilirubin 18.4 mg/dL, AST 488 U/L with AST/ALT above 2); corticosteroids are considered only once infection, GI bleeding and kidney injury are excluded or controlled (EASL ALD 2018).
Start enteral nutrition by nasogastric tube without protein restriction (1.2-1.5 g/kg protein per day) (EASL 2022).
Refer for liver transplant assessment: decompensated cirrhosis with recurrent overt HE, MELD-Na 36 (EASL 2018), together with addiction services for the alcohol relapse (EASL ALD 2018).

avoided_actions.rationale: No clinical suspicion for hepatopulmonary syndrome, portopulmonary hypertension, or endocarditis; echocardiography is not part of the HE workup.
Amyloid PET has no role in HE workup; reversible metabolic encephalopathy is the issue, not Alzheimer pathology.
DaTscan has no role in HE workup; the question is metabolic encephalopathy, not nigrostriatal degeneration.

accepted: Hepatic encephalopathy (West Haven grade IV), alcohol-related cirrhosis (Child-Pugh C, MELD-Na 36), precipitated by an alcohol binge with lactulose and rifaximin non-adherence, with hypokalemia (K 2.8 mEq/L) and hypoglycemia (glucose 58 mg/dL) as co-precipitants

differential.key_features: Concurrent possibility: binge drinking, whole-blood thiamine 22 nmol/L; the triad cannot be assessed in coma, though oculocephalic responses are full. Not excluded; thiamine is given empirically.

differential.diagnosis: Acute ethanol intoxication as the cause of the coma
differential.key_features: Ethanol 182 mg/dL contributes, but in a chronic heavy drinker it does not explain GCS 8 with fetor hepaticus, rigidity and triphasic waves; reassess as the ethanol clears.
Glucose 58 mg/dL is a co-precipitant but too mild to explain coma on its own.

differential.diagnosis: Superimposed severe alcohol-related hepatitis (acute-on-chronic liver failure)
differential.key_features: Recent heavy drinking, bilirubin 18.4 mg/dL, AST 488 U/L with AST/ALT above 2, CRP 14 mg/L: a cause of the decompensation, not an alternative to HE; to be assessed with hepatology.
Excluded: ascitic PMN 142 cells/mm3, Gram stain negative, culture no growth.
Unwitnessed collapse with INR 3.4 and platelets 48 raised the question; CT shows no hemorrhage.
Coma warranted the question; EEG shows reactive diffuse slowing with triphasic waves, without evolution or epileptiform discharges.

key_clinical_evidence: Child-Pugh C (15: bilirubin 18.4 3, albumin 1.8 3, INR 3.4 3, tense ascites 3, HE grade 4 3); MELD-Na 36 (creatinine 1.4, bilirubin 18.4, INR 3.4, sodium 128)

HE is a clinical diagnosis: West Haven grading, evidence of liver dysfunction and exclusion of other causes of altered mental status (ACG 2026; EASL 2022). Grade IV is coma; asterixis cannot be elicited in coma.

An elevated ammonia neither grades nor confirms hepatic encephalopathy and repeat levels are not used to guide treatment; a normal ammonia in a confused patient with cirrhosis should prompt a search for another cause (ACG 2026 recommendation 5 and key concept 14; EASL 2022).

Precipitant identification is more actionable than the ammonia number: infection (SBP especially), GI bleeding, electrolyte disturbance (hypokalemia, hyponatremia), constipation, sedatives, dehydration, kidney injury and non-adherence to lactulose and rifaximin (ACG 2026; EASL 2022).
Grade IV HE is coma: airway protection comes first, and lactulose is then given by nasogastric tube or enema.
In a malnourished heavy drinker, parenteral thiamine is given before or with glucose; Wernicke encephalopathy cannot be excluded clinically in coma (EFNS 2010).
Recurrent overt HE in decompensated cirrhosis is an indication for liver transplant assessment (EASL 2018).

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: In a chronic heavy drinker an ethanol of 182 mg/dL does not explain coma with fetor hepaticus, rigidity and triphasic waves; HE is the main cause, and lactulose, airway protection and the precipitant work-up must not wait for the ethanol to clear.
red_herrings.intended_effect: Attribute the coma to intoxication and observe while the alcohol clears.

eeg.impression: This is an ABNORMAL EEG due to: 1. Continuous generalized delta slowing at 1.0-2.5 Hz, high amplitude (180-240 µV), without a posterior dominant rhythm; the background attenuates to painful stimulation. 2. Frequent fronto-predominant triphasic waves at 1.0-2.0 Hz with an anterior-to-posterior phase lag of 30-50 ms, without evolution. No epileptiform discharges and no electrographic seizures. patient.history_present_illness: Mr. K. is a 48-year-old man with severe alcoholic cirrhosis (Child-Pugh C, MELD 24 at his admission three months ago) and a prior HE episode 3 months ago who was found unresponsive in his apartment by a neighbor. Emergency services report empty vodka bottles at the scene and the neighbor states the patient was found minimally responsive, unable to communicate; nobody saw him fall and the time he was last seen well is unknown. He had claimed sobriety since his outpatient detox 6 months ago. On arrival to the emergency department he has a GCS of 8: eyes open only to pain, incomprehensible sounds, and withdrawal from pain. He smells strongly of alcohol. He is profoundly icteric with massive tense ascites and fetor hepaticus. Blood pressure is 108/66 with tachycardia 104. His lactulose and rifaximin were likely not taken during the binge.

neurological_exam.additional: Severe jaundice. Massive tense ascites, abdomen markedly distended. Multiple spider angiomata on chest and face. Caput medusae visible on abdomen. Fetor hepaticus strongly present. Palmar erythema. No scalp laceration or hematoma seen. No fever. No neck stiffness. Paramedic states empty vodka bottles found at the apartment, suggesting recent heavy binge drinking.
neurological_exam.cranial_nerves: Pupils 4 mm bilaterally, equal, reactive. Oculocephalic (doll's eye) responses full. Corneal reflexes present. No facial asymmetry. Gag reflex present but reduced.
neurological_exam.mental_status: GCS 8 (E2V2M4). Eyes open to painful stimulation only. Incomprehensible vocalizations. Withdraws from pain in all four limbs. Does not follow commands. Orientation cannot be assessed. Asterixis cannot be tested because he cannot sustain a posture.
neurological_exam.motor: Withdraws all four limbs to pain, no lateralizing asymmetry. Increased tone (rigidity) in both lower limbs.
neurological_exam.reflexes: DTRs 2+ upper, 1+ lower. Bilateral plantar responses: equivocal.
